newsitem.title: USA: Clinton cabinet reshuffle may start this week.
newsitem.headline: Clinton cabinet reshuffle may start this week.

text.p: President Bill Clinton hoped to start forming his new cabinet by nominating a new secretary of state this week, the White House said on Tuesday, as signs grew that the reshuffle was causing turmoil and bruised egos.

Officials said former Sen. George Mitchell was the leading candidate to succeed Warren Christopher in the U.S. diplomatic hotseat, but some cautioned that U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright, Sen. Sam Nunn, perhaps retired Gen Colin Powell and other less-known candidates were also "still in play."
Christopher announced his departure last Thursday but will stay on until January.
Clinton was non-committal when asked by a reporter at a White House ceremony on Tuesday when he would name a replacement and whether it would be Mitchell.
"I haven't made a decision. I'm working on it. I'm working on a lot of appointments, and I will do it when I'm ready to do it. It's a very important decision," he said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the president was unlikely to make any cabinet announcements, "with the possible exception of secretary of state," before leaving on a 12-day trip to Asia on Friday.

One sign that the revamping of Clinton's team was causing turmoil was a senior official's disclosure that Deputy White House chief of staff Harold Ickes, a leading liberal in the administration and an architect of Clinton's re-election, had been effectively forced out of his job by incoming White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles.

Clinton called in Ickes last Friday, after he had decided to hire Bowles to replace departing White House chief of staff Leon Panetta, and told Ickes he could work elsewhere in the administration if he wanted, said the senior official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Ickes "was shown the door two days after the election," the official said. "Apparently Mr. Bowles made it a condition of his becoming chief of staff that (Ickes) had to leave."
Clinton was putting together his second-term lineup with a handful of trusted advisers, including Vice President Al Gore, Panetta, Bowles and Washington power-broker Vernon Jordan.
Mitchell, former majority leader when Democrats controlled the Senate, headed the list of candidates for secretary of state, administration officials said.
They said the Maine lawmaker had impressed Clinton when helping him to prepare for campaign debates with Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole.

Moreover, Mitchell is likely to be confirmed without difficulty by the U.S. Senate, a big plus for a White House anxious to avoid a repeat of the botched nominations that marred the start of Clinton's first term, officials said.

Officials said at the weekend Clinton had hoped to name his entire national security team before his trip, but that the process had gotten bogged down by a debate over how the team would fit together and whether to include a Republican.

Clinton has said that he wants his new Cabinet to be bipartisan, but sources familiar with the selection process said it was highly unlikely that someone from the opposition would get a high profile post such as State or Defence.
Officials said CIA Director John Deutch, former number-two official at the Pentagon, was a candidate to replace Perry.
